title: "Introduction: the Bayesian paradigm"
subtitle: "Lecture 1"
---

## Overview

By the end of this lecture you can turn a sample of monthly returns into a
probability distribution over the chance of a losing month, and state that chance
as a probability rather than as a confidence statement.

::: {.callout-important}
## The result of this chapter

For an unknown $\theta$ and observed data ${\bf x}$, the posterior is the
likelihood times the prior, renormalised,

$$
f(\theta \mid {\bf x}) \;\propto\; l(\theta \mid {\bf x})\, f(\theta),
$$

so every statement about $\theta$, point estimate, interval or forecast, is read
off a single distribution. The renormalising constant is an integral over the
parameter space, and whether that integral can be done in closed form is what
separates the conjugate models of the next two lectures from everything after
them.
:::

After working through this chapter you can

1. derive Bayes theorem for a parameter from the law of total probability;
2. diagnose what a frequentist confidence interval does and does not say about a
   parameter;
3. derive the Beta-Binomial posterior by recognising the kernel, without
   integrating;
4. interpret the posterior mean as a weighted average of prior and sample
   information, and predict how that weight moves with the sample size;
5. implement the update, the credible interval and the posterior predictive
   distribution in Python on real return data;
6. compare a Bayesian predictive forecast with the plug-in forecast that fixes
   the parameter at its estimate.

Week 1 of 15, paired with the [Week 1 exercise
session](../exercise-sessions/01-introduction.qmd). The chapter assumes only
introductory probability and a first course in statistics; nothing from later
chapters is needed.

## Motivation: what classical inference tells the investment committee {#sec-motivation}

An investment committee asks what probability it should attach to a negative
excess return on the US market portfolio next month. That single question is the
running example of this chapter, and every piece of machinery below is introduced
because the question needs it.

Write $L_t = 1$ if month $t$ delivers a positive excess return and $L_t = 0$ if it
does not, and let $\theta$ be the probability of a positive month, so that the
committee's number is $1 - \theta$. The twelve months of 2024 are a convenient
first sample, taken from the monthly file described in @sec-data: nine of them
were positive for the market portfolio and three, April, October and December,
were not. If months are conditionally independent given $\theta$, a positive month
contributes a factor $\theta$ to the probability of the observed sequence and a
negative month a factor $1 - \theta$, so

$$p(L_1,\ldots,L_{12}\mid\theta)=\theta^{9}(1-\theta)^{3}.$$

That is where a likelihood comes from. We counted outcomes; we did not pick a
distribution because it was convenient, and every assumption used is visible in
the counting: months are exchangeable, they share one $\theta$, and only the sign
of each month is recorded. Recording only the count nine rather than
the order of arrival would multiply the expression by a binomial coefficient,
which does not involve $\theta$ and will make no difference to anything below.

Classical inference now offers two things. The maximum likelihood estimate is the
sample frequency $\hat\theta = 9/12 = 0.75$, which puts the probability of a
losing month at one quarter. Around it comes a ninety-five percent confidence
interval, reported below in its exact Clopper-Pearson form because twelve
observations are far too few for the normal approximation.

```{python}
from pathlib import Path

import numpy as np
import pandas as pd
from scipy import stats
import matplotlib.pyplot as plt

from scipy.special import betaln, gammaln

DATA = next(p for p in (Path("data"), Path("../data")) if p.exists())

rng = np.random.default_rng(2026)
plt.rcParams.update({"figure.figsize": (7, 4.2), "axes.grid": True,
                     "grid.alpha": 0.3, "font.size": 11})

ff_m = pd.read_parquet(DATA / "ff_factors_monthly.parquet")
mkt = ff_m["mkt_rf"]                       # monthly market excess return
r24 = mkt["2024"]

n, y = len(r24), int((r24 > 0).sum())      # months observed and positive months
ci_lo = stats.beta.ppf(0.025, y, n - y + 1)
ci_hi = stats.beta.ppf(0.975, y + 1, n - y)

fig, ax = plt.subplots()
ax.bar(r24.index, 100 * r24.to_numpy(), width=20,
       color=np.where(r24.to_numpy() > 0, "tab:blue", "tab:red"))
ax.axhline(0.0, color="black", lw=1)
ax.set_ylabel("market excess return, percent")
ax.set_title("Twelve months of 2024: nine positive, three negative")
plt.tight_layout(); plt.show()

print(f"positive months {y} of {n}, sample frequency {y/n:.3f}")
print(f"95% confidence interval for theta: [{ci_lo:.3f}, {ci_hi:.3f}]")
print(f"implied point estimate of a losing month: {1 - y/n:.3f}")
```

The figure shows the twelve months in order, the three red bars being April,
October and December. The losses are not small: the worst of the three costs more
than four percent, which is why the committee cares about their frequency and not
only about the average return. The printed interval runs from $0.428$ to $0.945$,
so twelve months are compatible with a market that rises less often than a
coin and with one that rises almost always.

The committee wants to know how likely a loss is next month. It cannot get that
number from either output. The point estimate $0.25$ is a property of the twelve
months we happened to see, and nobody in the room believes the market loses
exactly a quarter of the time; twelve months are too few to separate the frequency
that turned up from the probability that generated it. A committee told that the
market rises three quarters of the time will size its positions accordingly, and
will be surprised at the first drawdown.

The interval is the more honest half of the classical output, and what it is
honest about is how little twelve months settle. But it looks like a probability
statement and is routinely read as one, as in "there is a ninety-five percent
chance that $\theta$ is between $0.43$ and $0.95$". That reading is wrong. It is
worth being precise about why, because the reason is not a matter of sample size
and no amount of extra data repairs it. Notice also what is not at fault. The
likelihood $\theta^{9}(1-\theta)^{3}$ was obtained by counting, it uses every
month we have, and nothing below will discard it. What the next section rejects is
the way classical inference turns that likelihood into a reported uncertainty, and
what @sec-methodology puts in its place leaves the likelihood untouched.

## The problem: a confidence interval is not a probability about the parameter {#sec-problem}

### Result R-1.1: what a frequentist interval is a statement about

Let ${\bf X}$ be data generated under a model indexed by a fixed unknown
$\theta \in \Theta$, and let $[L({\bf X}), U({\bf X})]$ be an interval estimator
with confidence level $1-\alpha$, meaning

$$
P_\theta\big(L({\bf X}) \le \theta \le U({\bf X})\big) = 1-\alpha
\qquad \text{for every } \theta \in \Theta .
$$

The probability is taken over ${\bf X}$ with $\theta$ held fixed. Once the data
are realised as ${\bf X} = {\bf x}$, the interval $[L({\bf x}), U({\bf x})]$ is a
pair of numbers and $\theta$ is a number, so

$$
\mathbf{1}\{L({\bf x}) \le \theta \le U({\bf x})\} \in \{0, 1\},
$$

and the coverage statement above says nothing about which of the two values it
takes. No enlargement of the sample changes this: increasing $n$ shrinks the
interval, but the object that carries the probability is still the random interval
and never the fixed $\theta$. To make a probability statement about $\theta$ one
needs a probability distribution over $\Theta$, which the frequentist framework
does not have.

A second symptom follows from the same source. Because the probability is taken
over data sets that might have been observed, the answer depends on which data
sets those are, that is, on the sampling plan, even when the observed data and the
likelihood are identical. Our twelve months of 2024 contain nine positive months,
and the classical test of $H_0: \theta = 0.5$ against $\theta > 0.5$ reports
$\sum_{k=9}^{12}\binom{12}{k}0.5^{12}$. Suppose instead the analyst had decided in
advance to watch the market until the third negative month and then stop. The
third negative month of 2024 was December, so this analyst records exactly the
same twelve months and exactly the same nine positive ones. The data are
identical; the sample space is not, since the number of months is now random and
the number of negative months is fixed, and the $p$-value changes with it.

The computation below makes both points at once. The loop draws two hundred
artificial samples of twelve months from a market with $\theta = 0.6$, builds the
same exact interval for each, and records which of them cover the true value; the
two $p$-values compare the sampling plans.

```{python}
theta_true, n_rep = 0.6, 200

y_rep = rng.binomial(n, theta_true, size=n_rep)
lo_rep = stats.beta.ppf(0.025, y_rep, n - y_rep + 1)
hi_rep = stats.beta.ppf(0.975, y_rep + 1, n - y_rep)
lo_rep, hi_rep = np.nan_to_num(lo_rep, nan=0.0), np.nan_to_num(hi_rep, nan=1.0)
covers = (lo_rep <= theta_true) & (theta_true <= hi_rep)

show = 60
fig, ax = plt.subplots()
for i in range(show):
    ax.plot([lo_rep[i], hi_rep[i]], [i, i], lw=1.4,
            color="tab:blue" if covers[i] else "tab:red")
ax.axvline(theta_true, color="black", lw=1)
ax.set_xlabel(r"$\theta$, probability of a positive month")
ax.set_ylabel("replicated sample"); ax.set_yticks([])
ax.set_title("Sixty 95% intervals from twelve months each; red ones miss")
plt.tight_layout(); plt.show()

print(f"coverage over {n_rep} replications: {covers.mean():.3f}")
print(f"width of the widest interval {np.max(hi_rep - lo_rep):.3f}, "
      f"narrowest {np.min(hi_rep - lo_rep):.3f}")

k = np.arange(y, n + 1)                    # binomial design: 9 or more positives in 12
p_binom = stats.binom.pmf(k, n, 0.5).sum()
j = np.arange(y, 60)                       # negative binomial design: 3rd negative in month 12
p_negbin = stats.nbinom.pmf(j, 3, 0.5).sum()
print(f"p-value, fixed number of months:          {p_binom:.4f}")
print(f"p-value, fixed number of negative months: {p_negbin:.4f}")
```

The figure is Result R-1.1 drawn. Each horizontal segment is the interval one
analyst would have reported from her own twelve months. The blue segments contain
the vertical line at the true value and the red ones do not; the confidence level
is a statement about the proportion of blue, which comes out at $0.980$ over the
two hundred replications, and about nothing else. The exact interval is
conservative in small samples, which is why the realised coverage sits above the
nominal $0.95$ rather than on it. Pick any single line in the picture and the
probability that it covers $\theta$ is zero or one. Our 2024 interval is one such
line, and we do not know its colour.

The widths make the same point from the other side. Across the two hundred
replications the widest interval spans $0.578$ and the narrowest $0.265$, so the
reported precision is itself a lottery: an analyst who happened to see eleven
positive months reports a much tighter interval than one who saw seven, and
neither of them can say that her own interval is the more trustworthy. The
probability lives in the procedure, before the data arrive, and once they have
arrived there is nothing left for it to describe.

The two $p$-values, $0.0730$ and $0.0327$, come from the same nine positive
months. At the conventional five percent threshold the first design does not
reject and the second does. The likelihood function is identical in both cases,
so a procedure that uses only the likelihood and a prior returns the same answer
either way. That procedure is the subject of the next section.

## Methodology: Bayes theorem and the Beta-Binomial update {#sec-methodology}

The repair is to give $\theta$ a distribution. The object we want, the probability
that $\theta$ lies in a stated range given the data in hand, then exists by
construction, and the rule that produces it is the one used for any other
conditional probability.

Two kinds of uncertainty have to be kept apart. Even if $\theta$ were known, next
month could go either way; on top of that, $\theta$ itself is unknown. The first
is handled by a conditional data model, the second by a prior distribution over
$\theta$. For a single month,
$P(L_t = 1 \mid \theta) = \theta$ and $P(L_t = 0 \mid \theta) = 1-\theta$ can be
written together as $p(L_t \mid \theta) = \theta^{L_t}(1-\theta)^{1-L_t}$, since
substituting $L_t = 1$ leaves $\theta$ and substituting $L_t = 0$ leaves
$1-\theta$. The exponents are a switch, not an extra assumption. Assuming
conditional independence across months with a common $\theta$, the probability of
the observed sequence is the product, and collecting powers gives
$\theta^{y}(1-\theta)^{n-y}$ for $y$ positive months out of $n$. Conditional
independence and a constant $\theta$ come from our model of the market, not from
Bayes theorem, and Lecture 8 drops them. Bayes theorem says how to update once a
model has been specified, not whether the model is right.

### Result R-1.2: Bayes theorem for a parameter

Let $\theta$ be an unknown parameter, of any dimension, and let ${\bf x}$ denote
the observed data. The likelihood $l(\theta \mid {\bf x}) = f({\bf x} \mid \theta)$
says how probable the observed data are for each candidate value of $\theta$, and
the prior $f(\theta)$ says what was believed about $\theta$ beforehand. Then

$$
f(\theta \mid {\bf x}) = \frac{f({\bf x} \mid \theta)\, f(\theta)}{f({\bf x})}
\;\propto\; l(\theta \mid {\bf x})\, f(\theta),
\qquad
f({\bf x}) = \int f({\bf x} \mid \theta) f(\theta)\, d\theta .
$$

The denominator $f({\bf x})$ is the marginal likelihood. It does not involve
$\theta$, so it only rescales the result, and in practice one works with the
proportionality and recovers the constant at the end. In words: the posterior is
the likelihood times the prior, renormalised. Unlike a confidence interval, the
left-hand side is a distribution over $\Theta$, so $P(\theta \in A \mid {\bf x})$
is defined for any set $A$ and is exactly what the committee asked for.

::: {.callout-note collapse="true"}
## Derivation

Start with events. Events $B_1, \dots, B_k$ form a partition of the sample space
if they are mutually exclusive and together exhaust every possibility, so exactly
one of them happens. For any event $A$ we can split $A$ according to which $B_i$
occurred,

$$
P(A) = P(A \cap B_1) + P(A \cap B_2) + \dots + P(A \cap B_k).
$$

The conditional probability of $A$ given $B$ is the share of $B$ in which $A$ also
happens, $P(A \mid B) = P(A \cap B) / P(B)$, which rearranged is the
multiplication law $P(A \cap B) = P(A \mid B) P(B)$. Substituting that into the
partition identity gives the law of total probability,

$$
P(A) = \sum_{j=1}^{k} P(A \mid B_j) P(B_j),
$$

with continuous counterpart $f(x) = \int f(x \mid y) f(y)\, dy$. Now write the
intersection $A \cap B_i$ in the two possible orders,
$P(A \mid B_i) P(B_i) = P(B_i \mid A) P(A)$, and replace $P(A)$ by the sum above
to obtain Bayes theorem for events,

$$
P(B_i \mid A) = \frac{P(A \mid B_i)\, P(B_i)}{\sum_{j=1}^{k} P(A \mid B_j)\, P(B_j)}.
$$

The parameter version is the same two steps with a density in place of a
probability and an integral in place of the sum. Write the joint density both
ways,

$$
f({\bf x}, \theta) = f({\bf x} \mid \theta) f(\theta)
= f(\theta \mid {\bf x}) f({\bf x}),
$$

divide by $f({\bf x})$ to get $f(\theta \mid {\bf x})$, and let the law of total
probability supply $f({\bf x}) = \int f({\bf x} \mid \theta) f(\theta)\, d\theta$.
:::

The direction of the conditioning is the part intuition gets wrong: a statement
about how often a warning appears among firms that default is not a statement
about how often a flagged firm defaults, and the two differ by the base rate that
the denominator supplies. Note also that the unknown need not be random in the
world for the rule to apply. A firm's default probability can be fixed while our
information about it changes, and it is the information that the posterior
describes.

### Result R-1.3: the Beta-Binomial posterior and its mean

For $y$ successes in $n$ conditionally independent Bernoulli trials with success
probability $\theta$ and prior $\theta \sim \text{Beta}(a,b)$, whose density is
$f(\theta) = \theta^{a-1}(1-\theta)^{b-1}/B(a,b)$ on $(0,1)$,

$$
\theta \mid y \sim \text{Beta}\!\left(a + y,\; b + n - y\right),
\qquad
\mathbb{E}[\theta \mid y] = \frac{a+y}{a+b+n},
$$

for any $n \ge 0$, any $0 \le y \le n$ and any $a, b > 0$. Writing $n_0 = a+b$ for
the prior sample size, $\theta_0 = a/n_0$ for the prior mean and
$\hat\theta = y/n$ for the maximum likelihood estimate, that mean is the weighted
average

$$
\mathbb{E}[\theta \mid y] = w\,\theta_0 + (1-w)\,\hat\theta,
\qquad w = \frac{n_0}{n_0+n} .
$$

::: {.callout-note collapse="true"}
## Derivation

Multiply likelihood by prior and drop every factor free of $\theta$,

$$
f(\theta \mid y) \;\propto\;
\underbrace{\theta^{y}(1-\theta)^{n-y}}_{\text{likelihood}}
\times \underbrace{\theta^{a-1}(1-\theta)^{b-1}}_{\text{prior}}
= \theta^{(a+y)-1}(1-\theta)^{(b+n-y)-1}.
$$

The right-hand side is the kernel of a beta density with parameters $a+y$ and
$b+n-y$. A density is determined by its kernel, so the normalising constant can be
read off rather than computed, and it must be $1/B(a+y,\, b+n-y)$. No integration
was performed anywhere.

For the mean, split the numerator as $a + y$ and divide each part by the common
denominator $n_0 + n$,

$$
\frac{a+y}{a+b+n}
= \frac{n_0}{n_0+n}\cdot\frac{a}{n_0} + \frac{n}{n_0+n}\cdot\frac{y}{n}
= w\,\theta_0 + (1-w)\,\hat\theta .
$$
:::

That is what conjugacy means: prior and posterior belong to the same family, so
updating is arithmetic on the parameters. Add the successes to $a$ and the
failures to $b$. It also fixes the interpretation of $a$ and $b$, since they enter
exactly as $y$ and $n-y$ do: the prior acts like a previous sample with $a$
imagined successes and $b$ imagined failures, of size $a+b$.

Two limits recur throughout the course. As $n \to \infty$ the weight $w \to 0$ and
the posterior mean converges to the classical estimate, so with enough data the
prior stops mattering. As $n_0 \to 0$ the prior becomes flat and the posterior
mean is the classical estimate immediately. The Bayesian machinery earns its keep
in between, which in economics and finance is nearly always where we are.

The same algebra also settles the order in which data may be processed. If a
second batch ${\bf y}$ arrives after ${\bf x}$, using $f(\theta \mid {\bf x})$ as
the prior gives
$f(\theta \mid {\bf x}, {\bf y}) \propto l(\theta \mid {\bf y})\,
f(\theta \mid {\bf x}) \propto l(\theta \mid {\bf y})\, l(\theta \mid {\bf x})\,
f(\theta)$, which is the posterior from pooling both batches against the original
prior. Yesterday's posterior is today's prior, and the order of arrival is
irrelevant. In the Beta-Binomial case the counts simply accumulate.

### Choosing the prior, and checking what it predicts

A prior is a probability distribution over the parameter before the current data
are seen, carrying information from theory, from previous studies, or a statement
that we know very little. There is no such thing as no prior: refusing to write
one down means defaulting to a flat prior, itself a strong choice.

| Type | Intent | Example |
|---|---|---|
| Informative | encode genuine knowledge | $\mathcal{N}(0.05, 0.02^2)$ on a monthly mean return |
| Weakly informative | rule out absurd values, stay vague | $\mathcal{N}(0, 1)$ on a standardised effect |
| Conjugate | keep the posterior in the same family | Beta prior for a binomial probability |
| Noninformative or Jeffreys | let the data dominate, invariance | $p(\theta) \propto \sqrt{I(\theta)}$ |

Conjugacy is a convenience, not a virtue: it makes the algebra close but matches
real beliefs only if its shape happens to. Because $a$ and $b$ enter the posterior
exactly as observed successes and failures do, elicitation can be phrased in
observable terms. One cannot ask a portfolio manager for $a$ and $b$, but one can
ask how many of the next hundred months she expects to be positive, which fixes
$a/(a+b)$, and how many months of experience her view is worth, which fixes $a+b$.
A manager who answers fifty and five hundred has specified a
$\text{Beta}(250,250)$ prior without hearing the word beta.

The honest final step is to feed the implications back, because a prior that
sounds reasonable in the parameter space can be absurd in the data space. The tool
is the prior predictive distribution,
$p(y) = \int p(y \mid \theta)\, p(\theta)\, d\theta$, which is the same integral as
the normalising constant in Result R-1.2, now read as the forecast of the data
implied by the prior alone. Sampling from it is immediate: draw $\theta$ from the
prior, then $y$ from the likelihood.

Noninformative priors such as $p(\theta) \propto 1$ on the real line or
$p(\sigma) \propto 1/\sigma$ on the positive line do not integrate to one. These
improper priors are often harmless, because the likelihood makes the posterior
proper, but for some models the posterior is improper too and then nothing
downstream means anything. For the binomial, Haldane's prior is
$f(\theta) \propto [\theta(1-\theta)]^{-1}$, the $a, b \to 0$ limit of the beta
family. Multiplying by the binomial likelihood gives
$f(\theta \mid y) \propto \theta^{y-1}(1-\theta)^{n-y-1}$, a proper
$\text{Beta}(y, n-y)$ distribution as long as $0 < y < n$. At the boundary it does
harm: in a year with twelve positive months one beta parameter is zero, the
posterior does not integrate, and every number computed downstream is meaningless.
The Jeffreys prior, $p(\theta) \propto \sqrt{I(\theta)}$ with $I(\theta)$ the
Fisher information, is the standard default, and its justification is invariance
under reparameterisation. For a binomial probability
$I(\theta) = n/[\theta(1-\theta)]$, so the prior is proportional to
$\theta^{-1/2}(1-\theta)^{-1/2}$, which is $\text{Beta}(1/2,1/2)$.

### Predicting the next months

A posterior answers a question about $\theta$, but the committee will eventually
ask about months rather than about a parameter. Prediction follows the same
integration logic. For a future observation $Y$ that is conditionally independent
of the past given $\theta$,

$$
f(y \mid {\bf x}) = \int f(y \mid \theta)\, f(\theta \mid {\bf x})\, d\theta ,
$$

so we average the sampling distribution over the posterior rather than plugging in
an estimate. For $m$ further months this has a closed form. Writing
$a^\star = a+y$ and $b^\star = b+n-y$ for the posterior parameters,

$$
P(Y = k \mid {\bf x}) = \int_0^1 \binom{m}{k}\theta^{k}(1-\theta)^{m-k}
\frac{\theta^{a^\star-1}(1-\theta)^{b^\star-1}}{B(a^\star,b^\star)}\, d\theta
= \binom{m}{k}\frac{B(a^\star+k,\; b^\star+m-k)}{B(a^\star,b^\star)},
$$

because the integrand is a beta kernel with parameters $a^\star+k$ and
$b^\star+m-k$, which integrates to $B(a^\star+k,\, b^\star+m-k)$ by definition of
the beta function. This is the beta-binomial distribution. The classical
alternative, $\text{Binomial}(m,\hat\theta)$, fixes $\theta$ at one value as if it
were known, and therefore reports a narrower forecast than the evidence
supports.

### Where conjugacy works, and where it stops

Conjugate priors exist for the exponential family, and the algebra is always the
one just done.

| Likelihood | Conjugate prior | Posterior |
|---|---|---|
| Binomial, $\theta$ | Beta$(a, b)$ | Beta$(a + y,\; b + n - y)$ |
| Poisson, intensity $\theta$ | Gamma$(a, b)$ | Gamma$(a + n,\; b + x)$ |
| Normal, mean $\mu$, known variance | Normal | Normal |
| Normal, precision $\tau$, known mean | Gamma | Gamma |
| Normal regression, $(\beta, \sigma^2)$ | Normal-inverse-gamma | Normal-inverse-gamma |

The Poisson row is worth deriving because Lecture 4 uses it and because it shows
that the recipe does not depend on the beta integral. If $n$ events are observed
over an exposure of length $x$, the likelihood for the intensity $\theta$ is
proportional to $\theta^{n} e^{-x\theta}$, and a $\text{Gamma}(a,b)$ prior is
proportional to $\theta^{a-1}e^{-b\theta}$. Multiplying and collecting,

$$
f(\theta \mid {\bf x}) \propto \theta^{n}e^{-x\theta}\cdot\theta^{a-1}e^{-b\theta}
= \theta^{(a+n)-1}e^{-(b+x)\theta},
$$

the kernel of a $\text{Gamma}(a+n, b+x)$ density. Add the event count to the shape
and the exposure to the rate, so $a$ is a prior number of events and $b$ a prior
exposure, and the posterior mean is again a weighted average, with weights
$b/(b+x)$ and $x/(b+x)$. Letting $a, b \to 0$ gives $f(\theta) \propto 1/\theta$.

Outside the exponential family the tidiness disappears. For a sample from a Cauchy
distribution, $f(x \mid \theta) = [\pi(1 + (x-\theta)^2)]^{-1}$, the likelihood
$\prod_i [1 + (x_i-\theta)^2]^{-1}$ multiplies into no standard prior to give a
recognisable family. The obstacle is not the multiplication but the
normalisation: to report anything we need
$f({\bf x}) = \int f({\bf x}\mid\theta) f(\theta)\, d\theta$, an integral with no
closed form. Everything from Lecture 3 onwards is a strategy for that integral,
either approximating it or sampling in a way that never requires it.

## Data: monthly US market excess returns, 1926 to 2026 {#sec-data}

The chapter's dataset is the monthly Fama-French factor file,
`data/ff_factors_monthly.parquet`, from the Kenneth French data library. The
column `mkt_rf` is the excess return on the value-weighted US market portfolio
over the one-month Treasury bill, the object the committee's question is about.
The file runs from July 1926 to July 2026 without gaps.

```{python}
n_all = len(mkt)
n_loss = int((mkt <= 0).sum())

fig, ax = plt.subplots()
ax.hist(100 * mkt[mkt > 0], bins=np.arange(-40, 42, 2), color="tab:blue",
        label="positive months")
ax.hist(100 * mkt[mkt <= 0], bins=np.arange(-40, 42, 2), color="tab:red",
        label="losing months")
ax.axvline(0.0, color="black", lw=1)
ax.set_xlabel("monthly market excess return, percent")
ax.set_ylabel("months"); ax.legend()
ax.set_title(f"{n_all} monthly excess returns, {mkt.index[0]:%Y-%m} to {mkt.index[-1]:%Y-%m}")
plt.tight_layout(); plt.show()

print(f"months {n_all}, from {mkt.index[0]:%Y-%m} to {mkt.index[-1]:%Y-%m}")
print(f"losing months {n_loss}, share {n_loss/n_all:.4f}")
print(f"mean {mkt.mean():.4f}, sd {mkt.std():.4f}, "
      f"worst {mkt.min():.4f}, best {mkt.max():.4f}")
```

The sample is the longest available for a broad equity index and runs across every
regime a committee might worry about, from the Depression to the inflation of the
1970s to the two drawdowns of this century. There are $1201$ months, of which
$472$ were losing months, a raw share of $0.3930$. The histogram shows why a single frequency is a crude summary of the
series: the distribution is roughly centred a little above zero, the red losing
months form a left portion with a long tail reaching almost to minus twenty-nine
percent, against a best month of plus thirty-nine percent,
and the average monthly excess return of $0.0069$ is small relative to a monthly
standard deviation of $0.0530$. The Bernoulli model of @sec-methodology keeps only
the sign of each bar and discards the magnitude, which is a deliberate
simplification and the first thing @sec-discussion revisits.

For the analysis the sample is split at the end of 1989. Everything up to December
1989 forms the prior, and the $439$ months from January 1990 to July 2026 are the
data we update on. That is what a Bayesian does when a long history exists but the
recent regime is the object of interest, and it uses the long record for the thing
a prior most needs, evidence from outside the sample being analysed. The split
date is a modelling choice and not a neutral one: it asserts that the pre-1990
market is informative about the modern one without being identical to it, which is
exactly the kind of belief a prior exists to encode. @sec-empirical reports how
much the answer would change if that belief were dropped altogether.

## Empirical analysis: the posterior probability of a losing month {#sec-empirical}

### The prior, and what it predicts

We now run Result R-1.3 on the data of @sec-data, in the order a working paper
would report it: the prior first, then the update, then the interval, then a
sensitivity check, then the forecast the committee actually wanted.

The pre-1990 record supplies the prior parameters directly, since by Result R-1.3
the numbers $a$ and $b$ enter exactly as counts of successes and failures. There
is nothing to elicit here, which is unusual and convenient: the two questions of
@sec-methodology, where is the prior centred and how many months is it worth, are
answered by the pre-1990 sample itself. Before using it, the prior is checked in
the data space.

```{python}
pre, new = mkt[:"1989-12"], mkt["1990-01":]
a_pre, b_pre = int((pre > 0).sum()), int((pre <= 0).sum())
y_new, n_new = int((new > 0).sum()), len(new)

n_sim, n_win = 20_000, 20
def prior_predictive_counts(a_p, b_p):        # draw theta from the prior, then a count
    return rng.binomial(n_win, stats.beta(a_p, b_p).rvs(n_sim, random_state=rng))

bins = np.arange(0, n_win + 2) - 0.5
fig, ax = plt.subplots()
ax.hist(prior_predictive_counts(a_pre, b_pre), bins=bins, density=True, alpha=0.6,
        label=f"history prior Beta({a_pre}, {b_pre})")
ax.hist(prior_predictive_counts(8, 2), bins=bins, density=True, alpha=0.6,
        label="overconfident prior Beta(8, 2)")
ax.set_xlabel("positive months out of 20"); ax.set_ylabel("prior predictive probability")
ax.legend(); ax.set_title("Different priors expect different data")
plt.tight_layout(); plt.show()

print(f"1926-1989: {a_pre} positive, {b_pre} losing months in {a_pre + b_pre}, "
      f"share {a_pre/(a_pre+b_pre):.4f}")
print(f"prior sample size a + b = {a_pre + b_pre}")
```

The prior is $\text{Beta}(451,311)$: $762$ months up to December 1989, of which
$451$ were positive and $311$ were losing months, a share of $0.5919$. Result
R-1.3 is being used in reverse here, reading the two beta parameters as the counts
they behave like. Its predictive distribution for the next
twenty months, the blue histogram, is centred near twelve positive months and puts
non-negligible mass on anything from about seven to seventeen, which is an honest
description of what sixty-three years of history imply about a twenty-month
window. The orange histogram is what a manager who claimed a $\text{Beta}(8,2)$
view would be committing to: seventeen positive months out of twenty as the
central case and barely a five percent chance of fewer than eleven. Stated in the
data space that claim is obviously too strong, and that is the point of the check.
The two densities are the same kind of object as the histogram in @sec-data,
counts of positive months, so a portfolio manager can be asked about them directly
and does not have to reason about a beta density she has never seen. The prior
sample size of $762$ is itself the number to argue about: it says the pre-1990
record should count for as much as $762$ fresh months, and anyone who thinks the
market changed in 1990 will want it smaller. The check below reports what happens
at the opposite extreme, where it counts for nothing at all.

### The update

```{python}
post = stats.beta(a_pre + y_new, b_pre + n_new - y_new)
w = (a_pre + b_pre) / (a_pre + b_pre + n_new)
mle = y_new / n_new

grid = np.linspace(0.50, 0.72, 400)
fig, ax = plt.subplots()
ax.plot(grid, stats.beta(a_pre, b_pre).pdf(grid), ":",
        label=f"prior Beta({a_pre}, {b_pre}), 1926-1989")
lik = stats.binom.pmf(y_new, n_new, grid)
ax.plot(grid, lik / np.trapezoid(lik, grid), "--", label="scaled likelihood, 1990-2026")
ax.plot(grid, post.pdf(grid), label=f"posterior Beta({a_pre+y_new}, {b_pre+n_new-y_new})")
ax.axvline(mle, color="grey", lw=1, label=f"1990-2026 frequency {mle:.3f}")
ax.set_xlabel(r"$\theta$, probability of a positive month")
ax.set_ylabel("density"); ax.legend(fontsize=9)
ax.set_title("The posterior sits between the prior and the likelihood")
plt.tight_layout(); plt.show()

print(f"1990-2026: {y_new} positive, {n_new - y_new} losing months in {n_new}, "
      f"frequency {mle:.4f}")
print(f"weight on the prior w = {w:.4f}")
print(f"posterior mean {post.mean():.4f} = "
      f"w*{a_pre/(a_pre+b_pre):.4f} + (1-w)*{mle:.4f} "
      f"= {w*a_pre/(a_pre+b_pre) + (1-w)*mle:.4f}")
```

The $439$ months from 1990 onwards contain $278$ positive months and $161$ losing
ones, a frequency of $0.6333$, so the recent regime looks kinder than the pre-1990
record by about four percentage points. Adding
counts gives the posterior $\text{Beta}(729,472)$, drawn as the solid curve, and
it lies between the dotted prior and the dashed likelihood exactly as Result R-1.3
requires. The weight on the prior is $w = 0.6345$, because $762$ prior months
outnumber the $439$ new ones, and the printed weighted average
$0.6345 \times 0.5919 + 0.3655 \times 0.6333$ reproduces the posterior mean
$0.6070$ to the last digit. The posterior is also visibly narrower than either
input, which is the whole point of combining them: $1201$ months constrain
$\theta$ better than $762$ or $439$ of them do.

Read as the committee's number, the posterior says the probability of a losing
month is $1 - 0.6070 = 0.3930$. It is worth pausing on how little the estimate
moved and how much the uncertainty shrank. The prior alone would have said
$0.4081$, the post-1990 data alone $0.3667$, and the combination lands at $0.3930$,
closer to the prior because the prior carries more months. The disagreement
between the two sources is about four percentage points, which is small enough
that the weighted average is uncontroversial; when a prior and a likelihood
disagree by much more than their widths, the right response is not to average them
but to ask which of the two is wrong, and Lecture 8 gives the tools for that.

### The credible interval and the committee's number

```{python}
lo, hi = post.ppf([0.025, 0.975])
a_s, b_s = a_pre + y_new, b_pre + n_new - y_new

print(f"posterior mean {post.mean():.4f}, median {post.median():.4f}, "
      f"mode {(a_s - 1)/(a_s + b_s - 2):.4f}")
print(f"95% equal-tailed credible interval for theta: [{lo:.4f}, {hi:.4f}]")
print(f"probability of a losing month: mean {1 - post.mean():.4f}, "
      f"interval [{1 - hi:.4f}, {1 - lo:.4f}]")
print(f"P(theta > 0.5 | data) = {1 - post.cdf(0.5):.6f}")
```

A credible interval is an interval $[\underline\theta, \overline\theta]$ with
$P(\underline\theta < \theta < \overline\theta \mid {\bf x}) = 0.95$, and it is
read off the posterior by quantiles rather than constructed from a sampling
distribution. The shortest such interval is the highest posterior density
interval; for a posterior as symmetric as this one the equal-tailed version used
below is almost identical, and the difference only becomes worth the extra work
when the posterior is skewed or has a boundary nearby. The interval for $\theta$
runs from $0.5792$ to $0.6344$, so the probability of a losing month is $0.3930$
with a range of $0.3656$ to $0.4208$. That sentence is a probability statement
about the parameter, which is what @sec-problem showed a confidence interval
cannot deliver: it refers to this interval, computed from these months, and not to
the long-run behaviour of a procedure. Mean, median and mode come out at $0.6070$,
$0.6071$ and $0.6072$, agreeing to three decimals because $1201$ effective
observations have made the posterior nearly symmetric. In a small sample they
would not agree, and which one to report is a question about the cost of being
wrong that Lecture 2 answers with a loss function rather than with a convention.

The last printed line is the kind of statement the framework licenses and the
classical one does not: the posterior probability that a month is more likely to
rise than to fall is $1.000000$ to six decimals. That is not a claim that the
market always rises. It is a claim about $\theta$, namely that after $1201$ months
essentially no posterior mass is left below one half, and it is the direct answer
to a question the $p$-values of @sec-problem could only approach sideways.

### How much does the prior matter?

```{python}
for name, (a_0, b_0) in {"history Beta(451,311)": (a_pre, b_pre),
                         "flat Beta(1,1)": (1, 1),
                         "Jeffreys Beta(0.5,0.5)": (0.5, 0.5)}.items():
    p = stats.beta(a_0 + y_new, b_0 + n_new - y_new)
    print(f"{name:>24}: posterior mean {p.mean():.4f}, "
          f"95% interval [{p.ppf(0.025):.4f}, {p.ppf(0.975):.4f}]")

for y_obs in (9, 12):            # Haldane prior: interior count and boundary count
    a_h, b_h = y_obs, 12 - y_obs
    print(f"Haldane, y = {y_obs:2d} of 12: Beta({a_h}, {b_h}) "
          f"{'proper' if a_h > 0 and b_h > 0 else 'IMPROPER, integrates to infinity'}")
```

Replacing the historical prior by a flat one moves the posterior mean from
$0.6070$ to $0.6327$, essentially onto the 1990-2026 sample frequency, and widens
the interval to $[0.5872, 0.6770]$ because $439$ months alone carry less
information than $1201$. The Jeffreys prior gives $0.6330$, indistinguishable from
the flat one at this sample size, which is the usual situation once $n$ is in the
hundreds. The Haldane lines are the warning from @sec-methodology made concrete:
with nine positive months out of twelve the improper prior still yields a proper
posterior, and with twelve out of twelve it does not, even though a simulation
would have happily returned numbers in both cases.

Two lessons are worth separating here. The first is that the prior matters, but in
a quantified way: the disagreement between the historical and the flat analysis is
two and a half percentage points in the mean and a widening of the interval from
$0.055$ to $0.090$, which is small enough to report as a robustness line and large enough that
hiding the prior would be dishonest. The second is that impropriety is not a
matter of degree. A posterior either integrates or it does not, and at the
boundary count no amount of computing power announces the failure.

### Forecasting the next twelve months

```{python}
m = 12
k = np.arange(m + 1)
log_choose = gammaln(m + 1) - gammaln(k + 1) - gammaln(m - k + 1)
pred = np.exp(log_choose + betaln(a_s + k, b_s + m - k) - betaln(a_s, b_s))
plug_in = stats.binom(m, post.mean()).pmf(k)

fig, ax = plt.subplots()
ax.bar(k - 0.18, pred, width=0.36, label="Bayesian predictive")
ax.bar(k + 0.18, plug_in, width=0.36, label=f"plug-in Binomial(12, {post.mean():.3f})")
ax.set_xlabel("positive months out of the next 12"); ax.set_ylabel("probability")
ax.legend(); ax.set_title("Parameter uncertainty widens the forecast")
plt.tight_layout(); plt.show()

sd = lambda p: np.sqrt((p * (k - (p * k).sum())**2).sum())
print(f"predictive mean {(pred*k).sum():.3f}, sd {sd(pred):.4f}")
print(f"plug-in    mean {(plug_in*k).sum():.3f}, sd {sd(plug_in):.4f}")
print(f"P(at least 6 losing months in 12): predictive {pred[:7].sum():.4f}, "
      f"plug-in {plug_in[:7].sum():.4f}")
```

Both forecasts are centred on $7.28$ positive months out of twelve, but the
predictive distribution is the wider of the two, with standard deviation $1.6997$
against $1.6919$ for the plug-in rule. The extra spread is the remaining
uncertainty about $\theta$ carried into the forecast instead of discarded. The gap
is small here precisely because $1201$ months have pinned $\theta$ down; with the
twelve months of @sec-motivation as the only evidence it would be large, and
ignoring it is the standard route to prediction intervals that are too narrow. The
probability of at least six losing months in the coming year is $0.3172$ under the
predictive distribution and $0.3164$ under the plug-in rule, a difference of less
than one part in four hundred.

The shape of the two bar charts is the thing to remember rather than the size of
the gap. The Bayesian predictive distribution is the beta-binomial of
@sec-methodology, which integrates $\theta$ out rather than fixing it, so its
spread contains both sources of uncertainty: the coin flip that any month is, and
our residual doubt about how the coin is weighted. The plug-in binomial contains
only the first. Here the second is nearly exhausted, which is why the bars almost
coincide, and that is itself a result worth stating to the committee: after a
century of monthly data, what limits the forecast is the randomness of markets and
not our ignorance of $\theta$. In the twelve-month sample of @sec-motivation the
ordering would be dramatic rather than decorative, and in the regression models of
Lecture 2, where a handful of coefficients and a variance are all uncertain at
once, the gap is large enough to change a risk number.

### Updating never starts over

```{python}
up = (new > 0).to_numpy().astype(int)
fig, ax = plt.subplots()
for k_obs in [0, 12, 60, 240, n_new]:
    s = int(up[:k_obs].sum())
    ax.plot(grid, stats.beta(a_pre + s, b_pre + k_obs - s).pdf(grid),
            label=f"after {k_obs} months")
ax.axvline(mle, color="black", lw=1, ls=":", label="1990-2026 frequency")
ax.set_xlabel(r"$\theta$"); ax.set_ylabel("posterior density")
ax.legend(fontsize=9); ax.set_title("The posterior concentrates as months accumulate")
plt.tight_layout(); plt.show()

half = n_new // 2
s1, s2 = int(up[:half].sum()), int(up[half:].sum())
seq = stats.beta(a_pre + s1 + s2, b_pre + n_new - s1 - s2)
print(f"two-step update: Beta({a_pre}, {b_pre}) -> "
      f"Beta({a_pre + s1}, {b_pre + half - s1}) -> Beta({seq.args[0]}, {seq.args[1]})")
print(f"one-step update: Beta({a_s}, {b_s})")
print(f"posterior means agree: {seq.mean():.6f} vs {post.mean():.6f}")
```

Feeding the months in one batch or two gives the identical posterior
$\text{Beta}(729,472)$, as the algebra at the end of Result R-1.3 promised, and
the two printed means agree to six decimals. The figure shows the same fact as a
sequence: the curve for zero months is the prior, and each further batch of months
pulls it towards the 1990-2026 frequency and narrows it. The movement is slow
because the prior is worth $762$ months, so even $439$ new observations shift the
centre by only about one and a half percentage points, from $0.5919$ to $0.6070$.

The five curves also make the weight formula of Result R-1.3 visible as a
sequence. After twelve months the posterior is indistinguishable from the prior,
because $w = 762/774$ leaves almost nothing for the data; after sixty months the
weight on the prior is still $0.93$ and the curve has barely moved; only by $240$
months, with $w = 0.76$, does the centre shift visibly, and the full $439$ months
bring it to $0.6345$. A student who expects new data to overturn a prior quickly
should read the numbers on this figure, because the arithmetic is the same in
every conjugate model in the course.

The practical content of this is larger than the picture suggests. Nothing in the
calculation required the $439$ months to be available at once, and nothing
required them in date order: the intermediate posterior $\text{Beta}(585,396)$
after the first $219$ months is a complete summary of everything seen so far, and
the second half of the sample updates it without revisiting a single earlier
observation. A risk system can therefore carry two numbers rather than a data
history, and a calculation split across machines and recombined gives the same
answer as one run in sequence. This exactness is a property of conjugate models
and of sufficient statistics; from Lecture 3 onwards, where posteriors are
represented by samples rather than by two parameters, updating remains conceptually
sequential but stops being free.

## Discussion: one probability now, three exposures next {#sec-discussion}

The committee asked how likely a loss is next month, and the answer is $0.393$,
with a ninety-five percent credible interval from $0.366$ to $0.421$. The sentence
means what it appears to mean: given this model, this prior and these $1201$
months, the probability that $\theta$ lies in that range is $0.95$. After a
century of data the monthly win rate is still uncertain by about five percentage
points, which is a useful corrective to anyone quoting such a figure to three
decimals, and the predictive distribution turns it into the statement the
committee can act on, namely a $0.317$ chance of at least six losing months in the
coming year.

What the committee should do with that number depends on what it costs to be
wrong, and the posterior is the right input to that decision rather than a
substitute for it. A mandate that forbids more than five losing months in twelve
is, on these numbers, violated roughly one year in three, which is a fact about
the market and not about the manager. The interval matters as much as the point:
a rule calibrated to a losing rate of $0.366$ and a rule calibrated to $0.421$ are
different rules, and the data cannot presently distinguish them. The one thing the
number is not is a claim about size. The Bernoulli model keeps only the sign of
each month, so a year of twelve small losses and a year with one crash of nearly
twenty-nine percent are the same observation to it, and @sec-data showed that the
loss distribution has a long left tail that the sign discards. Any serious risk
statement needs the magnitudes as well, which means a model of returns and not of
signs.

Before trusting the machinery it is worth checking that the closed form is not
doing anything mysterious. Bayes theorem says only that the posterior is
proportional to likelihood times prior. Evaluating that product on a grid and
dividing by its sum replaces the integral by a sum; drawing from the posterior and
averaging replaces it by a sample mean. Both should reproduce the analytic answer.

```{python}
theta_grid = np.linspace(0, 1, 2001)
unnorm = stats.binom.pmf(y_new, n_new, theta_grid) * stats.beta(a_pre, b_pre).pdf(theta_grid)
dens = unnorm / np.trapezoid(unnorm, theta_grid)          # normalise numerically
grid_mean = np.trapezoid(theta_grid * dens, theta_grid)

draws = post.rvs(size=20_000, random_state=rng)
mc_loss = (1 - draws).mean()
mc_se = draws.std(ddof=1) / np.sqrt(draws.size)

fig, ax = plt.subplots()
ax.hist(1 - draws, bins=60, density=True, alpha=0.5, label="Monte Carlo, 20,000 draws")
ax.plot(1 - theta_grid, dens, label="grid posterior")
ax.plot(1 - grid, post.pdf(grid), "--", label="analytic Beta posterior")
ax.set_xlim(0.34, 0.45)
ax.set_xlabel(r"$1-\theta$, probability of a losing month"); ax.set_ylabel("density")
ax.legend(fontsize=9); ax.set_title("Grid, simulation and algebra agree")
plt.tight_layout(); plt.show()

print(f"analytic posterior mean {post.mean():.6f}")
print(f"grid posterior mean     {grid_mean:.6f}")
print(f"Monte Carlo mean        {draws.mean():.6f}  (standard error {mc_se:.6f})")
print(f"largest error in the grid density: {np.abs(dens - post.pdf(theta_grid)).max():.2e}")
print(f"Monte Carlo P(losing month) {mc_loss:.4f} vs analytic {1 - post.mean():.4f}")
```

The three curves lie on top of each other, and the grid mean matches the analytic
mean to six decimals, with a largest pointwise error of $1.78 \times 10^{-13}$ in
the density itself, while the Monte Carlo mean, $0.607107$, differs from it by
$0.000113$, the size of its own reported standard error of $0.000100$. The
comparison is worth making in that direction. The Monte Carlo answer is not exact
and does not pretend to be; what it reports alongside the estimate is how wrong it
is likely to be, and that self-assessment is accurate here because we can check it
against algebra. From Lecture 3 onwards there is no algebra to check against, and
the standard error is the only warning available, which is why it is introduced
now in a case where its honesty can be verified.

That agreement is reassuring and also a little misleading, because the grid
works here only since $\theta$ is one-dimensional and bounded. A grid with five
hundred points per dimension needs $500^{10}$ evaluations for ten parameters,
which is why the course moves from grids to sampling rather than to finer grids.

Two limitations remain, and they point in different directions. The first is that
the model was taken as given: the committee might reasonably ask whether the data
support any departure from an even chance at all, which compares two models rather
than estimating one parameter. Bayes theorem answers that too, one level up, with
marginal likelihoods, posterior odds and Bayes factors in place of likelihoods,
and Lecture 9 states and uses that machinery.

The second limitation is the binding one. A losing month is a single probability,
and a single probability was enough to make every calculation above closed form.
The committee's next question is not. It will ask how much of the portfolio's
return is compensation for market risk, for size and for value, which is three
unknown exposures at once, and it will ask them about a return whose variance is
itself unknown. That is a five-dimensional posterior, not a one-dimensional one,
and counting successes will not produce it. Lecture 2 builds it: the linear
regression model with a Normal-inverse-gamma prior, where the same rule,
posterior proportional to likelihood times prior, is applied to
$\beta \mid \sigma^2 \sim \mathcal{N}(b_0, \sigma^2 B_0)$ and
$\sigma^2 \sim \text{IG}(\alpha_0, \delta_0)$, and where the posterior mean turns
out to be the same weighted average seen in Result R-1.3, now in matrix form.

## Exercises

These are the chapter's practice questions; the [Week 1 exercise
session](../exercise-sessions/01-introduction.qmd) works through them and adds the
lab.

1. By hand. Derive the Poisson-Gamma posterior of @sec-methodology from scratch,
   then show that its mean is a weighted average of the prior mean $a/b$ and the
   maximum likelihood estimate $n/x$, and identify the weight. State what happens
   as the exposure $x$ grows and as $a, b \to 0$.

2. Computational. Take the $\text{Beta}(451,311)$ prior and the $439$ months from
   1990 onwards. Recompute the posterior with a grid of $50$, $200$ and $2000$
   points and report the largest absolute error in the posterior mean for each.
   Then repeat the exercise with a prior that is a fifty-fifty mixture of
   $\text{Beta}(451,311)$ and $\text{Beta}(2,2)$, for which no single conjugate
   update applies, and compare the two posterior means.

3. On real data. Using the same file, define a losing month for the size factor
   `smb` instead of the market. Elicit a prior by the two-question method of
   @sec-methodology, justify it in two sentences, compute the posterior, the
   ninety-five percent credible interval and the predictive probability of at
   least six losing months in the next twelve, and say in one paragraph whether
   the prior or the data is driving your answer.

Exercise 1 is the one to attempt before the session, since it is the only place
where you will meet a conjugate pair that is not the Beta-Binomial, and Lecture 4
assumes it. Exercises 2 and 3 are written for the session itself and reuse the
code of @sec-empirical with two lines changed.

## Reading and references

The probability rules, conjugacy, prior elicitation and sequential updating in
@sec-methodology follow UPM Classes 1 and 2. The order of presentation, general
statement first and the Bernoulli example carried through, follows SGPE Lecture 1,
which also supplies the model comparison machinery referenced in
@sec-discussion and stated in full in Lecture 9. Greenberg (2008), Chapters 2 to
4, provides the bridge from probability to inference, and the confidence interval
diagnosis of @sec-problem is standard; Chapter 4 of Lambert gives a longer version
of the same argument. The data are the monthly factors of the Kenneth French data
library, distributed with this course as a repository snapshot.

Result R-1.1 is deliberately stated in the notation those sources use for
interval estimators, so that the contrast with the credible interval of
@sec-empirical is a contrast of definitions and not of symbols. Readers who want
the philosophical argument at greater length will find it in Chapter 1 of Gelman
et al.; readers who want only the algebra can read Result R-1.2 and Result R-1.3
and go straight to Lecture 2.

The explanations and exercises are adapted to this course's notation and weekly
structure; consult the cited originals for the full treatments.

Koop, *Bayesian Econometrics*, ch. 1. Zellner, *An Introduction to Bayesian
Inference in Econometrics*, ch. 1-2. Gelman et al., *Bayesian Data Analysis* (3rd
ed.), ch. 1-2. Lambert, *A Student's Guide to Bayesian Statistics*, ch. 1-5.
